title: Superhero Fatigue and the Return of the Event Movie

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: After Endgame, the shared-universe formula wears thin, while Top Gun, Avatar, Dune and Nolan prove that audiences still want spectacle, as long as it feels one of a kind.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: When Avengers: Endgame (2019) became the highest-grossing film in history in 2019, the model built by Kevin Feige seemed invincible: dozens of interconnected films, released at an industrial pace, each one promising the next. The pandemic interrupted the calendar, but not the formula. In December 2021, with the pandemic still raging, Spider-Man: No Way Home (2021) brought Tom Holland together with the Spider-Men of Tobey Maguire and Andrew Garfield and turned nostalgia into an event. The film crossed $1 billion in just 12 days, without even opening in China, and finished with about $1.92 billion, the biggest box office of 2021. It was the old machine's last great peak and, in hindsight, also its turning point: from then on, the genre that had dominated the previous decade would begin to show signs of fatigue.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The problem began with volume. With Disney+ up and running since 2019, Marvel started producing for two screens at once. The so-called Phase Four, launched by the series WandaVision on January 15, 2021, comprised seven films, eight series and two specials in less than two years, an output that led even the entertainment press to ask whether the studio still had a map. For the average viewer, every new movie started to feel like homework: you had to have watched the series to know who was who. Behind the scenes, the strain showed too. In September 2023, Marvel's visual effects artists voted unanimously to unionize, complaining of tight deadlines, unpaid overtime and overwork on the franchise's films and series. The machine kept turning, but ever faster and with ever less care.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: In 2023, the cracks became impossible to hide. Ant-Man and the Wasp: Quantumania (2023), which kicked off Phase Five in February, grossed $476 million and suffered the steepest second-weekend drop in the franchise's history in the U.S.: 69%. In November, Nia DaCosta's The Marvels (2023) made just $206 million worldwide, the lowest gross in the Marvel Cinematic Universe and the brand's first outright flop. Weeks later, Disney CEO Bob Iger publicly admitted the mistake of ramping up production to feed streaming: in Marvel's case, he said, “quantity diluted quality,” and the studio had made too many sequels. The year ended with another blow: in December, Jonathan Majors, who played Kang, the villain meant to anchor the entire new saga, was fired after being convicted of assault, and Marvel had to redraw its plans.

segments.original: Meanwhile, DC was in an even deeper crisis. The universe launched by Zack Snyder stumbled to an end, and The Flash (2023), released in June 2023 after years of director changes and the controversies surrounding Ezra Miller, grossed only $271 million against an estimated budget of $200 million to $220 million. Warner Bros. Discovery had already decided to start from scratch: in October 2022, James Gunn, director of Guardians of the Galaxy, and producer Peter Safran were named heads of the new DC Studios, tasked with planning an entire universe — films, series and animation — under a single creative vision. Even outside the shared universes, the warning lights were flashing: Joker: Folie à Deux (2024), the sequel to a film that had crossed $1 billion in 2019, made about $208 million in 2024, little more than it cost.

tracks.title: Learn more: Superman (2025): rebooting a universe

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Learn more: Superman (2025): rebooting a universe.
segments.text: Learn more: Superman, from twenty twenty-five: rebooting a universe.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: When they took over DC Studios on November 1, 2022, James Gunn and Peter Safran had a task rare in Hollywood: erase an entire universe and start another without losing the audience along the way. On January 31, 2023, they unveiled the first chapter of the new plan, dubbed Gods and Monsters. The official debut came with the animated series Creature Commandos in December 2024, but the cornerstone was Superman (2025), released in the U.S. on July 11, 2025. Written and directed by Gunn, the film starred David Corenswet as an optimistic, vulnerable Superman, alongside Rachel Brosnahan as Lois Lane and Nicholas Hoult as Lex Luthor, plus Krypto the dog, inspired by the director's own pet. Colorful and earnest, it was well received by critics and grossed $618.7 million, the biggest superhero box office of 2025, though far from the heights of the previous decade. The reboot, however, is not a sure thing: in June 2026, Supergirl (2026) had a weak opening, and Safran admitted the result fell short of the studio's expectations. The sequel, Man of Tomorrow, is slated for 2027.

segments.original: It was against this backdrop that the phrase “superhero fatigue” became the stuff of headlines, panel discussions and analyst reports. But the numbers told a more complicated story. In July 2024, Deadpool & Wolverine (2024), Marvel Studios' only theatrical release that year, teamed up Ryan Reynolds and Hugh Jackman, mocked the studio's own crisis and grossed $1.34 billion, becoming the highest-grossing R-rated film in history up to that point. In 2025, by contrast, Marvel released three films that landed between $380 million and $522 million, even when critics liked them: Captain America: Brave New World (2025), Thunderbolts* (2025), one of the best-reviewed entries of the new phase, and The Fantastic 4: First Steps (2025), which opened Phase Six. Feige himself admitted, in July 2025, that the studio had overextended itself in Phases Four and Five.

segments.original: While the shared universes spun their wheels, another kind of film was winning back theaters: the event film, the kind audiences feel they have to see on the biggest screen possible. The founding case was Joseph Kosinski's Top Gun: Maverick (2022). Originally slated for 2019 and postponed several times, first to finish the action sequences and then because of the pandemic, the film drew offers from streaming platforms, all of them turned down by Tom Cruise, who insisted on an exclusive theatrical release. The aerial scenes were shot for real, with IMAX-certified cameras mounted inside the cockpits of F/A-18 fighter jets, yielding more than 800 hours of flight footage. Released in May 2022, it grossed about $1.5 billion, the biggest box office of Cruise's career. At the end of that same year, James Cameron's Avatar: The Way of Water (2022) reached $2.33 billion, betting on 3D, IMAX and high-frame-rate projection.

segments.original: The summer of 2023 cemented the thesis. On the same day, July 21, Greta Gerwig's Barbie (2023) and Christopher Nolan's Oppenheimer (2023) opened, and audiences, swept up by the Barbenheimer meme, treated the double release as a must-see outing: Barbie reached $1.44 billion and Oppenheimer, a three-hour historical drama, nearly $1 billion, with more than $17 million coming from just 30 screens equipped to show IMAX 70mm film. In 2024, Denis Villeneuve's Dune: Part Two (2024), delayed by the Hollywood strikes, opened in March exclusively in theaters and grossed $715 million, about 20% of it from IMAX screens. The lesson was clear: moviegoers who had grown used to waiting for any film to hit streaming were once again willing to pay more for a ticket when the screening promised something their TV at home couldn't deliver.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The new generation of events also came from places Hollywood had long treated as second-tier. Video games, for decades synonymous with failed adaptations, turned into gold: The Super Mario Bros. Movie (2023) grossed $1.36 billion in 2023, and A Minecraft Movie (2025) scored the biggest U.S. opening ever for a video game adaptation and reached $961 million. Animation drove the box office like no other genre: Inside Out 2 (2024) took in $1.7 billion in 2024 and became, at the time, the highest-grossing animated film in history, and Moana 2 (2024), which began life as a Disney+ series and was turned into a feature midway through production, crossed $1 billion. That reversal of Marvel's path says a lot about the decade: what had been platform content became a theatrical release once again.

segments.original: The most symbolic success, however, came from the least expected place: an original film. Ryan Coogler's Sinners (2025) blended vampire horror, the blues and the history of the 1930s American South, was shot on 65mm with IMAX and Ultra Panavision 70 cameras, and grossed about $370 million worldwide. It was the first original film to top $200 million in the domestic market since Coco in 2017. Coogler also struck a rare deal with Warner: final cut, a share of the box office from the first dollar and ownership of the film after 25 years. Its crowning moment came at the 2026 Oscars, with a record 16 nominations, as told in the chapter on horror. For Hollywood, the message was a different one: a director with an idea of his own could also become an event, with no franchise behind him.

segments.original: The year 2026 summed up the decade. Released on July 17, Nolan's The Odyssey crossed $1.6 billion and took from Deadpool & Wolverine the title of highest-grossing R-rated film in history. Two weeks later, Destin Daniel Cretton's Spider-Man: Brand New Day (2026) posted the second-biggest worldwide opening of all time ($927 million) and within three weeks became only the eighth film to top $2 billion. Superheroes hadn't died: the same character who closed out the old era came back almost five years later treated as an event, not as just another chapter. Now Marvel is betting everything on Avengers: Doomsday (2026), directed by the Russo brothers and with Robert Downey Jr. back, this time as Doctor Doom, the villain who took Kang's place; it is set to open in U.S. theaters on December 18. The lesson of these years is that audiences never tired of spectacle. They tired of the formula.

tracks.title: Learn more: IMAX: the theater as the selling point

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Learn more: IMAX: the theater as the selling point.
segments.text: Learn more: IMAX: the theater as the selling point.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: For decades, IMAX was associated with museum documentaries. In the 2020s, it became the place where blockbusters are won or lost. With just over 1,800 screens worldwide, a tiny fraction of the circuit, the company closed 2025 with a record $1.28 billion at the box office, 13% above its previous best year, 2019. Christopher Nolan turned the format into a signature, and The Odyssey (2026) was the first feature shot entirely on IMAX film cameras. Tickets for the 70mm screenings went on sale on July 17, 2025, a year before the release, and some sold out in under 12 hours. Only 41 screens in the world could show that version, and IMAX even refurbished old projectors and trained new projectionists to meet demand. In August 2026, the film became the highest-grossing release in IMAX history, surpassing the first Avatar. In a market where almost everything reaches streaming within a few weeks, the theater itself became the selling point.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The return of the event neatly closes an era that began with the screens going dark. In March 2020, theaters around the world shut down, and many people bet that streaming had won for good. Five years later, screenings of The Odyssey were selling out a year ahead of release. Along the way, cinema changed shape: it learned to be born from memes and YouTube channels, saw horror and films in languages other than English move to the center, went on strike over streaming and artificial intelligence, and watched major studios merge. What didn't change was the reason to leave the house. In an age when almost everything fits on a phone screen, the movie theater survived by becoming the home of what doesn't fit there: spectacle seen together, in the dark, as an event.
